items.prompt: What is the name of the clear, curved surface at the very front of the eye that light passes through first?

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: Correct. The cornea is the transparent, dome-shaped layer at the front of the eye; it does most of the initial bending of light.

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: The lens is behind the pupil and iris, not at the very front. Light reaches it after passing through the cornea.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is at the back of the eye, where the image forms. It is not the first surface light touches.

options.label: The sclera
options.feedback: The sclera is the white, tough outer coat of the eye. It is not transparent and is not at the front center.

items.ok_line: The cornea is the transparent front surface.
items.ko_line: Remember what light meets first at the front of the eye.
items.exp_text: The cornea is the transparent, curved layer that covers the iris and pupil. It is the first thing light encounters when it enters the eye, and its shape helps focus the light before it goes deeper.

items.prompt: What is the colored ring of muscle in the eye that controls how much light enters through the pupil?

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, not the colored ring at the front.

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: The lens sits behind the iris and focuses light, but it is not the colored part you see.

options.label: The iris
options.feedback: Correct. The iris is the colored ring of muscle; it changes size to adjust the pupil's opening.

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: The cornea is the clear front cover, not the colored ring. It does not control light entry.

items.ok_line: The iris is the colored muscle controlling pupil size.
items.ko_line: The iris is the ring that gives your eye its color and adjusts light.
items.exp_text: The iris is the circular muscle that gives the eye its color. By contracting or relaxing, it changes the size of the pupil, the black hole in the center, to let more or less light in.

items.prompt: In the retina, what are the two main types of light-sensitive cells called?

options.label: Cones and cylinders
options.feedback: Cylinders are not a real cell type in the retina. The correct partner to cones is rods.

options.label: Rods and cones
options.feedback: Correct. Rods work in dim light and see black and white, while cones see color in bright light.

options.label: Bipolar and ganglion cells
options.feedback: These are nerve cells that carry signals from the retina, not the ones that detect light directly.

options.label: Pigment and lens cells
options.feedback: Lens cells are not in the retina, and pigment cells do not detect light; they support the retina.

items.ok_line: Rods and cones are the two light-sensitive cells.
items.ko_line: Only rods and cones respond to light itself in the retina.
items.exp_text: The retina has two kinds of photoreceptor cells: rods, which are very sensitive to dim light but only see in shades of gray, and cones, which work in bright light and detect color. Together they form the picture of what you see.

items.prompt: What is the small, yellow-colored area in the center of the retina that gives the sharpest, clearest vision?

options.label: The optic nerve
options.feedback: The optic nerve carries signals from the eye to the brain, but it is not where the sharpest vision happens.

options.label: The blind spot
options.feedback: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it has no light-sensitive cells, so you cannot see there.

options.label: The pupil
options.feedback: The pupil is the opening in the iris, not a part of the retina.

options.label: The fovea
options.feedback: Correct. The fovea is the tiny, central pit of the retina packed with cones, giving the sharpest detail.

items.ok_line: The fovea is the retina's center for fine detail.
items.ko_line: Only the fovea provides the clearest vision in the retina.
items.exp_text: The fovea is a small depression in the middle of the retina, packed almost entirely with cones. Because of its dense cone population, it produces the sharpest and most detailed vision, which is why you move your eyes to look directly at something.

items.prompt: What is the jelly-like substance that fills the large space behind the lens and helps keep the eyeball's shape?

options.label: The vitreous humor
options.feedback: Correct. Vitreous humor is the clear, jelly-like gel that fills the main cavity of the eye.

options.label: The aqueous humor
options.feedback: Aqueous humor is the watery fluid in the front chamber, between the cornea and lens, not the main back space.

options.label: The choroid
options.feedback: The choroid is a layer of blood vessels between the retina and the sclera, not a filling substance.

options.label: The lens capsule
options.feedback: The lens capsule is a thin membrane around the lens, not the jelly filling the eyeball.

items.ok_line: Vitreous humor is the jelly inside the eyeball.
items.ko_line: Only vitreous humor fills the large back chamber of the eye.
items.exp_text: Vitreous humor is a clear, gel-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina. It helps keep the eyeball round and firm, and it lets light pass through to reach the retina without distortion.

items.prompt: What does the lens of the eye do to light that passes through it?

options.label: It absorbs the light to prevent glare
options.feedback: The lens does not absorb much light; it focuses it. Glare is not its job.

options.label: It blocks harmful rays completely
options.feedback: The lens filters some ultraviolet light, but its main job is not blocking rays; it's focusing light.

options.label: It bends and focuses the light onto the retina
options.feedback: Correct. The lens changes shape to bend light rays so they meet sharply on the retina.

options.label: It converts the light into electrical signals
options.feedback: Converting light to signals happens in the retina's cells, not in the lens.

items.ok_line: The lens focuses light onto the retina.
items.ko_line: The lens only bends light; it does not convert or block it.
items.exp_text: The lens is a flexible, transparent structure behind the iris. It changes its curvature to bend incoming light rays, bringing them together to form a sharp image on the retina. By adjusting its shape, it lets you focus at different distances.

items.prompt: What is the name of the light-sensitive layer of nerve tissue that lines the back and sides of the inside of the eye?

options.label: The sclera
options.feedback: The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eye, not the light-sensitive inner layer.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: Correct. The retina is the inner lining of the eye that detects light and starts the visual signal.

options.label: The choroid
options.feedback: The choroid is a blood-vessel layer between the retina and sclera, not the light detector itself.

options.label: The iris
options.feedback: The iris is the colored front ring, not the back lining of the eye.

items.ok_line: The retina is the eye's inner light detector.
items.ko_line: Only the retina senses light and sends signals to the brain.
items.exp_text: The retina is a thin, multi-layered sheet of nerve tissue covering the inner back of the eyeball. Its photoreceptor cells, rods and cones, capture light and convert it into electrical signals that travel along the optic nerve to the brain.

items.prompt: What is the name of the nerve that carries visual information from the eye to the brain?

options.label: The auditory nerve
options.feedback: The auditory nerve carries hearing information, not sight. The eye uses a different nerve.

options.label: The olfactory nerve
options.feedback: The olfactory nerve carries smell information from the nose, not from the eye.

options.label: The trigeminal nerve
options.feedback: The trigeminal nerve senses touch and pain in the face, not visual information.

options.label: The optic nerve
options.feedback: Correct. The optic nerve connects each eye to the brain and carries the signals from the retina.

items.ok_line: The optic nerve sends sight signals to the brain.
items.ko_line: Only the optic nerve carries vision from the eye.
items.exp_text: The optic nerve is a bundle of nerve fibers that gathers signals from the retina's cells and transmits them to the visual processing areas of the brain. It exits the back of the eye at the blind spot, where there are no photoreceptors.

items.prompt: What is the small, black circular opening in the center of the iris that lets light enter the eye?

options.label: The pupil
options.feedback: Correct. The pupil is the dark central opening; it widens and narrows to control light entry.

options.label: The macula
options.feedback: The macula is an area of the retina, not an opening at the front of the eye.

options.label: The fovea
options.feedback: The fovea is the central pit of the retina, not a visible opening in the iris.

options.label: The optic disc
options.feedback: The optic disc is the blind spot where the optic nerve leaves, not the front opening.

items.ok_line: The pupil is the black opening in the iris.
items.ko_line: Only the pupil is the entrance for light at the eye's front.
items.exp_text: The pupil is the round, black hole in the middle of the iris. It looks black because light entering it is absorbed inside the eye. The iris muscles change its size—small in bright light, large in dim light—to regulate how much light passes through.

items.prompt: What is the white, tough outer layer of the eyeball that gives it its shape and protects it?

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is the inner light-sensitive layer, not the outer protective coat.

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: The cornea is the clear front part of the outer layer, not the whole white covering.

options.label: The sclera
options.feedback: Correct. The sclera is the white, fibrous outer covering that protects the eye and maintains its shape.

options.label: The choroid
options.feedback: The choroid is a blood-rich layer between the retina and sclera, not the outer coat.

items.ok_line: The sclera is the tough white outer layer.
items.ko_line: Only the sclera forms the white protective shell of the eye.
items.exp_text: The sclera is the dense, white, connective tissue that covers most of the eyeball. It gives the eye its firm shape, anchors the muscles that move it, and protects the delicate internal structures. At the front, it becomes the transparent cornea.
